Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Ravi leaned forward in the chair, his hands pressed flat against his thighs as if to steady himself. At twenty-four, he was the youngest diplomat in his country’s consulate, a position he had earned through relentless ambition and a fluency in three languages. He had been in the field for only eight months when his convoy was caught in a mortar attack on a road outside the city. The explosion had thrown him from the vehicle, and for what felt like an eternity he lay facedown in the dirt, the acrid smell of burning fuel and something metallic filling his nostrils. He remembered the silence afterward, then the shouting, and the way his own breath came in short, ragged gasps he could not control. He had not been physically wounded, but something had shifted inside him that day, and he had not been able to name it until much later.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi found himself unable to speak about what had happened. He knew the sequence of events perfectly—the sudden stop, the flash, the heat—but when colleagues or his girlfriend, Priya, asked him how he was doing, the words would not come. It was as if the experience existed in a place inside him that had no language. At night, the memory returned with startling clarity: the precise shade of the sky, the texture of the gravel against his cheek, and most disturbingly, the smell. He would be standing in the consulate kitchen, and suddenly the scent of cooking oil would shift, and he would be back on that road, his heart hammering, his skin cold. He had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him, that he had somehow caused the attack to happen, or that he had failed to prevent it. He had lost his faith in the idea that the world was orderly or that people could be trusted to keep him safe.

At work, Ravi began to change. He stopped taking the stairs, preferring the elevator because it was enclosed and he could control who entered. When strangers approached him in the hallway—visitors, contractors, even new staff—his chest would tighten and he would scan the room for exits. His supervisor noticed he was avoiding the open-plan reception area, choosing instead to work from a small windowless office at the back. Ravi told himself it was more efficient, but privately he was certain that if he could make himself less visible, he would be less of a target. He started wearing darker, looser clothing—jackets with high collars, shirts in muted colors—so that he would not draw attention. He stopped going to the gym because it felt too exposed, but he began running alone at night, pushing himself until his legs burned and his lungs ached, as if he could outrun the feeling of vulnerability that clung to him.

The smell of alcohol became a particular problem. He had never been a heavy drinker, but after the attack, even the faint odor of beer on a colleague’s breath at a consulate reception would send him reeling. He began declining social invitations, then avoiding them altogether. Priya grew frustrated, then worried. She did not understand why he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, or why he insisted on sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants. He could not explain it to her. What frightened him most was the flashbacks—moments when he would be standing in line at the grocery store or sitting at his desk, and suddenly he was back on that road, his body bracing for an impact that had already happened. He had started using cannabis in the evenings to dull the edges, telling himself it was just to sleep, but the doses crept higher.

What finally brought Ravi to the clinic was a morning in the consulate garage. A car backfired as he walked past, and he dropped to the ground, his hands over his head, shaking. A security guard found him there and helped him up, but Ravi could see the confusion in the man’s eyes. He knew he could not keep living like this. He was terrified that he had no future, that he would always be this person—jumpy, withdrawn, unable to trust the safety that everyone around him insisted was real. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him find a way back to the person he had been before the explosion, though he was not sure that person existed anymore.
